t.5.33.1: Having heard that account of Rāma from the bull among monkeys, Vaidehī spoke these soothing words in a sweet voice.
t.5.33.2: Where did your association with Rāma come about? How do you know Lakṣmaṇa? And how did the meeting of monkeys and men take place?
t.5.33.3: O monkey, tell me once more the marks of Rāma and of Lakṣmaṇa, so that grief may not overwhelm me.
t.5.33.4: What is his build like, and what is the form of Rāma like? What are his thighs like, what are his arms like? Tell me also of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.5.33.5: Thus addressed by Vaidehī, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, then began to describe Rāma just as he truly was.
t.5.33.7: O large-eyed one, hear from me as I speak of those marks of Rāma, and those too of Lakṣmaṇa, that have been observed.
t.5.33.6: Ah, how fortunate, O Vaidehī, that though you know them yourself, you question me, O lotus-petal-eyed one, about the distinguishing marks of your husband and of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.5.33.8: O daughter of Janaka, Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, who captivates the hearts of all beings, and who is endowed with beauty and courtesy, was born into this world.
t.5.33.9: In splendor he is like Āditya, in forbearance equal to Pṛthivī, equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom, and like Vāsava in renown.
t.5.33.10: He is the protector of the world of living beings and the protector of his own people; that scorcher of foes is the protector of his own conduct and of dharma.
t.5.33.11: O lovely lady, Rāma is the protector of the world and of the four varṇas; he is the one who establishes the bounds of right conduct for the world, and who causes them to be observed.
t.5.33.12: He is radiant and exceedingly honored, steadfast in the vow of celibacy; he knows how to render service to the virtuous and understands the proper conduct of deeds.
t.5.33.13: He is trained in the science of kingship and is one who honors and serves the brāhmaṇas; learned, endowed with good character, and disciplined, he is a scorcher of his foes.
t.5.33.14: He is trained in the Yajurveda and highly honored by those who know the Vedas; he is firmly grounded in the science of archery, in the Veda, and in the Vedāṅgas.
t.5.33.15: Broad-shouldered and mighty-armed, with a neck shaped like a conch and a handsome face, his collarbones hidden in flesh and his eyes deep copper-red, such is Rāma, O queen, as people know him.
t.5.33.16: His voice resounds like the beating of a kettledrum; his complexion is glossy and he is full of splendour. Well-proportioned, with evenly balanced limbs, he has a dark complexion.
t.5.33.17: He is firm in three parts, long-hanging in three, even in three and raised in three; he bears three folds, is bent low in three, is short in four, and has three whorls upon his head.
t.5.33.18: He bears four auspicious marks and four lines, stands four cubits tall, and is even in four parts of his body; his fourteen pairs of limbs are evenly matched, he has four fine teeth, and he moves with a fourfold gait.
t.5.33.20: Devoted to truth and righteousness, glorious, delighting in gathering people to himself and bestowing favour upon them, knowing the proper divisions of place and time, he speaks kindly to all the world.
t.5.33.19: Rāghava has a large lip, jaw and nose; he is glossy in five parts and has eight long limbs. He has ten lotus-like features and ten large ones, is endowed with three, and has two white features. He is elevated in six parts and slender in nine, and he pervades with three.
t.5.33.21: And his brother born of another mother, Saumitri the unconquered, is of the same kind in devotion, in beauty, and in virtues as well.
t.5.33.22: Searching for you alone as they wandered over the earth, those two saw the lord of the forest creatures, who had been deposed by his elder brother.
t.5.33.23: On the slope of Ṛśyamūka, thick with many trees, they came upon Sugrīva, handsome to behold, sitting there, distressed by his brother over his wife.
t.5.33.24: We, however, attend upon that king of the monkeys, Sugrīva, true to his promise, who was driven from his kingdom by his elder brother.
t.5.33.25: Then those two, clad in bark garments and holding excellent bows in their hands, arrived at a lovely region of the mountain Ṛśyamūka.
t.5.33.26: Seeing those two tigers among men bearing bows, that bull among monkeys, bewildered by fear, leapt up onto the peak of that mountain.
t.5.33.27: Then the lord of the monkeys, stationed upon that peak, swiftly sent me alone into the presence of those two.
t.5.33.28: At Sugrīva's bidding, I approached with joined palms those two lords, tigers among men, endowed with beauty and auspicious marks.
t.5.33.29: Once I had fully learned the true purpose of those two bulls among men, who were filled with goodwill, I lifted them onto my back and carried them to that place.
t.5.33.30: And the two were truthfully introduced to the great-souled Sugrīva, and from their conversing with one another a deep affection arose between them.
t.5.33.31: There those two renowned ones, the lord of the monkeys and the lord of men, gave comfort to each other by recounting what had happened to them before.
t.5.33.32: Then the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa consoled Sugrīva, who had been cast out on account of a woman by his brother Vālin of great might.
t.5.33.33: Then Lakṣmaṇa made known to Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, the grief of Rāma, of unwearied deeds, born of your loss.
t.5.33.34: But that lord of the monkeys, having heard the words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, then became utterly lusterless, like the sun seized by a planet.
t.5.33.35: Then those many ornaments that graced your limbs, which you let fall upon the ground as you were being carried off by the rākṣasa…
t.5.33.36: The leaders of the monkey troops brought all of those to Rāma and, delighted, showed them to him, but they did not know where you had gone.
t.5.33.37: Those jingling ornaments that lay scattered on the ground were gathered up by me alone and given to Rāma, while he was stricken in mind.
t.5.33.38: Then, having placed those lovely things in his lap, that lord, radiant as a god, lamented in many ways.
t.5.33.40: And that great-souled one, stricken with grief, lay there for a long time; and I too, with many kinds of words, raised him up again with difficulty.
t.5.33.39: As Dāśarathi gazed at them again and again, weeping and growing faint, those things of hers kindled the fire of his grief.
t.5.33.42: O noble lady, because he cannot see you, that Rāghava is constantly tormented, as a volcano is by a great blazing fire.
t.5.33.41: Having seen those precious ornaments and having shown them again and again, Rāghava, together with Saumitri, made them known to Sugrīva.
t.5.33.43: On your account, sleeplessness, grief and anxiety torment that great-souled Rāghava, as fires heat a fire-sanctuary.
t.5.33.44: Rāghava is shaken by grief at not seeing you, as a great mountain is shaken by a mighty earthquake.
t.5.33.46: O daughter of Janaka, Rāghava, that tiger among men, having slain Rāvaṇa together with his friends and kinsmen, will swiftly reach you.
t.5.33.45: Roaming through the most delightful forests, the rivers and the cascading springs, he finds no joy, for he has not seen you, O daughter of the king.
t.5.33.48: Then Rāma, having swiftly slain Vālin in battle, made Sugrīva the lord of all the hosts of bears and monkeys.
t.5.33.49: Thus, O queen, came about the alliance between Rāma and Sugrīva. And know me to be Hanūmān, their messenger, who has come here.
t.5.33.47: Then Rāma and Sugrīva, both joined together, made a pact: to slay Vālin, and likewise to search for you.
t.5.33.50: Having regained his own kingdom, Sugrīva gathered the great monkeys and, for your sake, sent those mighty ones out in all ten directions.
t.5.33.51: Commanded by Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, those mighty ones, resembling the king of mountains, set out in every direction across the earth.
t.5.33.52: The glorious and mighty son of Vālin, named Aṅgada, a tiger among monkeys, set out surrounded by a third part of the army.
t.5.33.53: While we were lost on the Vindhya, the finest of mountains, utterly overwhelmed by grief, many days and nights went by.
t.5.33.54: Despairing of accomplishing our task, because the appointed time had passed, and out of fear of the king of the monkeys, we were resolved to give up our lives.
t.5.33.55: Having searched the impenetrable forests and the mountain streams, and failing to find any trace of the queen, we resolved to give up our lives.
t.5.33.56: Sunk deep in an ocean of grief, Aṅgada lamented, O Vaidehī, your loss and likewise the slaying of Vālin, our resolve to fast unto death, and the death of Jaṭāyus.
t.5.33.58: The king of vultures named Saṃpāti, the uterine brother of the king of vultures, having heard of his brother's slaying, spoke these words out of anger.
t.5.33.57: To us, who because of our master's command were without hope and longing to die, there came a great and mighty bird, as though for the sake of our mission.
t.5.33.59: By whom was my younger brother slain, and where was he destroyed? This I wish to have told to me by you, O best of monkeys.
t.5.33.60: Aṅgada told him exactly as it happened of the great slaying in Janasthāna, carried out on your account by the demon of fearsome form.
t.5.33.62: Having heard those words of Saṃpāti, which increased our joy, all of us monkeys, led by Aṅgada, then set out, delighted and content, our zeal roused by the prospect of seeing you.
t.5.33.61: But on hearing of the slaying of Jaṭāyu, that son of Aruṇa, stricken with grief, told of you, O lady of beautiful hips, dwelling in the abode of Rāvaṇa.
t.5.33.63: Then, shaking off the intense fear of the monkey army, which was losing heart at the sight of the ocean, I leapt across a hundred yojanas.
t.5.33.64: And Laṅkā too, teeming with rākṣasas, was entered by me at night; and Rāvaṇa was seen by me, and you too, tormented by grief.
t.5.33.65: All this has been told to you just as it happened, O blameless one. Speak to me, O queen; I am the messenger of Dāśarathi.
t.5.33.66: O Devī, know me to be the son of the Wind-god, the counsellor of Sugrīva, who has undertaken this effort on Rāma's behalf and has come here for your sake.
t.5.33.67: Your Kākutstha, the foremost of all who bear weapons, is well, and so is Lakṣmaṇa of auspicious marks, devoted to the service of his elder.
t.5.33.68: O Devī, devoted to the welfare of that valiant lord of yours, I alone have come here at the command of Sugrīva.
t.5.33.69: This southern quarter has been traversed by me, roaming alone, able to assume any form at will, and eager to search out your trail.
t.5.33.71: By good fortune, O queen, my leap across the ocean has not been in vain; by good fortune I shall win this glory that comes from having seen you.
t.5.33.70: By good fortune I shall remove the anguish of the monkey hosts, who grieve over your loss, by announcing my meeting with you.
t.5.33.72: And Rāghava of mighty valour will swiftly come to you, having slain Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, together with his friends and kinsmen.
t.5.33.73: O Vaidehī, there is a mountain named Kauraja, the finest of mountains. From there the monkey Kesarī went to Mount Gokarṇa.
t.5.33.74: My father, that great monkey, was seen by the divine seers at the holy tīrtha of the lord of rivers, and he destroyed Śambasādana.
t.5.33.76: Thus reassured by these reasons and by the fitting tokens of recognition, Sītā, emaciated by grief, recognized him as a messenger.
t.5.33.75: In the field of that monkey I was begotten by the Wind, O Maithilī, and I am renowned in the world as Hanumān through my own deeds. It was to win your trust, O Vaidehī, that I spoke of your husband's virtues.
t.5.33.77: Jānakī, having attained incomparable joy through her great delight, shed tears born of bliss from her eyes with their curving lashes.
t.5.33.78: And that lovely face of the large-eyed lady, with its long eyes of coppery red and white, shone like the lord of the stars released from Rāhu. She now clearly took him to be the monkey Hanūmān, and not otherwise.
t.5.33.79: Then Hanumān spoke a reply to her, the one lovely to behold.
t.5.33.80: When the asura Śambasādana had been slain in battle by that foremost of monkeys at the urging of the great sages, I was then born of Vāyu, O Maithilī, a monkey equal to him in might.
